title: Stapleton denies the calumny: penitents should by certain trust, not by infallible faith, judge sins remitted
source_text: XXVIII. Praesertim vero expressa est hac de re Stapletoni doctrina, lib. 9. de Justif. cap. 20. ubi postquam questus est Catholicis per calumniam a Protestantibus tribui, quod doceant peccatorem in seria poenitentia & vera fide constitutum, nec posse, nec debere certa fiducia statuere peccata sibi remitti: posse quidem bene sperare, & de Dei misericordia optima quaeque sibi polliceri; sed haec tamen sine certa fiducia in medio fluctuantis dubitationis suspensa esse relinquenda, quia fidei possit subesse falsum, & spes possit fallere, sic inter alia suorum sententiam exponit: Non negamus, inquit, debere poenitentes certa fiducia statuere sibi remitti peccata; sed negamus certa fide, cui subesse falsum non potest, hoc esse a quoquam statuendum. Certam autem fiduciam, qualem spei certitudo affert, agnoscimus & docemus. Et postea, Non relinquimus peccatorem in medio fluctuantis dubitationis suspensum, postquam poenitentiae rite peractae sibi conscius est. Et cap. sequenti, loquens de Patribus & de Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae, Docent, inquit, vere poenitentes, & qui suam indispositionem serio corrigunt, non debere de remissione peccatorum suorum dubitare, sed certa fiducia confidere.
pass_a_gloss: But especially express is Stapleton’s doctrine on this matter in On Justification, book 9, chapter 20, where after he has complained that it is attributed to Catholics by calumny from the Protestants that they teach a sinner constituted in serious repentance and true faith neither can nor ought by certain trust to establish that sins are remitted to him—that he can indeed hope well and promise himself the best things from God’s mercy, but that these things without certain trust are to be left suspended in the midst of fluctuating doubt, because falsehood can underlie faith and hope can deceive—he thus among other things sets out the opinion of his own: We do not deny, he says, that penitents ought by certain trust to establish that sins are remitted to them; but we deny that this is to be established by anyone with certain faith, to which falsehood cannot be subject. But certain trust, such as the certainty of hope brings, we acknowledge and teach. And afterward: We do not leave the sinner suspended in the midst of fluctuating doubt after he is conscious to himself of repentance duly performed. And in the following chapter, speaking of the Fathers and of the doctors of the Roman Church: They teach, he says, that the truly penitent, and those who seriously correct their indisposition, ought not to doubt concerning the remission of their sins, but to trust with certain trust.
pass_b_english: Stapleton rejects the charge that Catholics strand penitents in endless doubt.
Penitents should judge sins remitted by certain trust of hope, not by infallible faith-certainty.
